## Leviticus 14:29–57: research notes

### vv. 29–32 (the poor leper's offerings, finished)

**v. 29**
- The leftover oil was put on the head, the way priests and kings were anointed. Guzik (Enduring Word) says this told the restored leper that God in some sense saw him as a king and a priest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/
- Guzik also notes the repeated phrase "him who is to be cleansed." In one sense the leper was already cleansed; in another he was still being cleansed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/
- Guzik says the oil rite for the poor man was the same as the full rite in vv. 15–18. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/
- Matthew Henry (on vv. 10–20): wherever Christ's blood is applied for justification, the Spirit's "oil" is applied for sanctification. The two can't be separated. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/leviticus-14.html

**vv. 30–31**
- Guzik (on vv. 21–23): many lepers would have been poor after long exclusion, and God graciously let birds replace two of the three lambs. The poor man still came to the same place and the same priests as the rich man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/
- Gill (on v. 23): the poor leper went through the same rites as the rich one. Being poor did not excuse him from duty or cost him any privilege. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-14.html
- Coffman: poverty did not waive the main parts of the cleansing, which were the male lamb for the guilt offering and the log of oil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-14.html
- What the offerings meant (Constable, on vv. 10–32): the sin offering cleansed the sanctuary, the burnt offering stood for reconciliation and rededication, and the grain offering was a pledge of allegiance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-14.html
- Guzik quotes Rooker on the parallel vv. 19–20: the sin offering put a person right with God, and the burnt and grain offerings stood for renewed devotion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: provision was made so that even the poorest had no excuse for neglecting cleansing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-14.html
- Precept Austin lists a Joseph Parker sermon on 14:30, "Such as He can get" (title only; not read). https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_14_resources

**v. 32**
- Gill: the first part of the chapter covers the leper who could afford the full rite, and this part covers the poor one. He cites a Jewish rule: a poor leper may bring a rich man's offering, but a rich leper may not bring a poor man's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-14.html

### vv. 33–53 (mildew or "leprosy" in a house)

**v. 33 (the section as a whole)**
- William Kelly sees the leprosy of the house as plainly "corporate evil." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-34.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says these rules are not health laws, as Lange held. Following Keil, it says they rest on a symbolic basis. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/leviticus-14.html
- Barnes: leprosy in houses, clothing and bodies were forms of decay. They taught that created things pass away and last only as long as the Lord sustains them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/leviticus-14.html

**v. 34**
- **Looking ahead:** Israel lived in tents in the wilderness, so this law was added as an appendix for life in Canaan (Benson; JFB). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-14.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/leviticus-14.html
- Coffman notes the change from "outside the camp" to "outside the city." He calls it fanciful to use this to date the passage later. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-14.html
- **What "I put" means. Readings differ here:**
  - *A direct act of God.* Gill says this kind of leprosy came from God's immediate hand and was miraculous. He reports Jewish teaching that it struck only Israelite houses in Canaan (not Gentile houses, not Jerusalem) and came because of the owner's sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-34.html
  - Benson calls it a special judgment on this people, or a special help toward repentance. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-14.html
  - *God's providence.* JFB says many read it as punishment for the owner's sins. Others note that Scripture often says God does what he only permits. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/leviticus-14.html
  - Enduring Word likewise offers that it may be a Hebrew way of saying God ultimately directs or allows all things. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/
  - The Geneva Study Bible: no plague comes to anyone apart from God's providence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/14-34.htm
  - Matthew Henry: if no natural cause can be found, put it down to the God of nature, compare Zechariah 5:4. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-34.html
  - *Not passed on from people.* One comment on Biblehub's page (writer not named in the excerpt) says "I put" disproves Knobel's view that house-leprosy spread from a leper to the walls. The occupants are never called unclean. The same page reports a Second Temple–era Jewish tradition that house-leprosy struck owners who built with stolen materials. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/14-34.htm
  - Constable agrees that God "put" the condition there; it didn't simply spread by contagion. He adds that the law reminded Israel that their homes, not just their bodies, should be holy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-14.html
- Guzik says the "plague" covers a broad range of things, including mold, mildew and fungus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/

**v. 35**
- Henry: the owner is expected to tell the priest at the first sign. "Sin, where that reigns in a house, is a plague there." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-36.html
- Henry: those in charge of others should catch trouble early, before it spreads. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-34.html

**v. 36**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the house was emptied so the furniture would not become ritually unclean, and "not… lest it should convey contagion." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-36.html
- The NET note (quoted on Precept Austin): once the priest declared the house unclean, everything in it was unclean too. Emptying it beforehand saved the contents. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_14_commentary
- Benson: nothing became unclean until the priest found and declared the problem. This shows God makes a difference between sins of ignorance and sins against knowledge. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-14.html
- Haydock (Catholic, 1811): the contents could be used freely afterward unless signs later appeared on garments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-36.html

**v. 37**
- **NET notes (scholarship):** the Hebrew word translated "depressions" is uncertain. Suggestions are "depressions" (LXX, Targums, NIV), "streaks" (ASV, NJPS), or "eruptions" (from an Egyptian loanword). "Wall" here means the plaster surface. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Lev&chapter=14&verse=37
- Benson: these were hollow streaks like those on leprous bodies. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-14.html

**v. 38**
- The Biblical Illustrator gives a natural explanation. Shutting the house up without air or light created ideal conditions for dry rot, so seven days would show whether it was real. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-36.html

**vv. 39–42**
- Ellicott: if the mark had spread after a week, the affected stones were removed, just as with leprous people and garments (Lev 13:5). They went to the unclean dump outside the city. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/14-39.htm
- Henry: this was like cutting off a gangrened limb to save the rest of the body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-34.html
- Everett (v. 40): in Jerusalem, this unclean place later became the Valley of Hinnom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/leviticus-14.html
- Biblehub's own study note on v. 39: the seven-day wait meant restoring holiness was not rushed. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/14-39.htm

**vv. 43–45**
- Guzik on v. 44: he quotes Peter-Contesse that "active leprosy" means roughly a fungus that cannot be got rid of. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-14.cfm
- Pulpit (v. 45): just as the leper was removed from the camp, the leprous house is pulled down completely. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/leviticus-14.html
- Henry: better to have no house than live in an infected one. Stubborn sin will in the end ruin families and churches. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-35.html
- Henry also says leftover sin in our bodies is like this: we're never fully rid of it until "the earthly house of this tabernacle" is taken down (Rom 6:7). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-36.html
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: houses that can't be cleansed are destined to be destroyed. It applies this to the final removal of uncured depravity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-14.html
- Biblehub study note (v. 44): unchecked sin makes lives and communities unfit for God's presence. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/14-44.htm
- **Applied to the church (a Protestant–Catholic point):** the Pulpit Commentary's homilies read the house as a church or community (1 Tim 3:15). They list corruption in doctrine, worship and morals, using the churches of Galatia, Corinth and Revelation as examples. One homily points to a church selling "indulgences" as a house badly struck with leprosy. This is a polemic clearly aimed at Rome. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/leviticus-14.html

**vv. 46–47**
- Gill: a shut-up house could stay closed for at most three weeks (Rashi). He cites Mishnah detail: putting even your head inside made you unclean. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-46.html
- Pulpit: the uncleanness was mild, ending at evening after washing clothes. Such a rule would have done nothing to stop infection, so preventing infection was not its purpose. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/leviticus-14.html
- Guzik: anyone entering a quarantined house had to take the proper measures. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-14.cfm

**v. 48**
- JFB: the precautions show how dangerous house-leprosy was in hot countries. A formal declaration of "clean" calmed public fears and relieved the owner. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/leviticus-14.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/14-53.htm
- Henry: the house had to be ritually purified as well as aired, so an Israelite could live in it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-53.html

**vv. 49–53 (the two-bird rite for the house)**
- **Same rite as the leper's, but no sacrifices.** Ellicott: this repeats vv. 3–7, minus the later sacrifices, which a house could not bring. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/14-49.htm
- Constable: no sacrifices were needed because buildings simply have to be clean. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-14.html
- Gill: the birds are implied to be living and clean. The sprinkling was on the upper doorpost, and the rites alone made the house fit to live in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/14-49.htm
- **The materials.** The Geneva Study Bible thinks the scarlet was a cord tying the hyssop to the wood to make a sprinkler (compare Heb 9:19, "scarlet wool"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/leviticus-14.html
- The NET note says the phrase means literally "crimson of worm," and that "living water" means flowing water. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_14_commentary
- **"Cleanse" and "make atonement" for a house (vv. 52–53).** Barnes: the word strictly means "purge … from sin," and is used figuratively when applied to things. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/leviticus-14.html
- JFB: a house can't be impure before God, so the "atonement" refers either to the occupants' sins or to the ritual itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/14-49.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the aim was to purify the house of sin's uncleanness. Sin starts in the human body but spreads to what people touch and live in, though not as physical contagion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/14-49.htm
- Henry, citing Bishop Patrick: the house was struck for the owner's sake, and the owner should see himself as spared by God's mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-36.html
- **What the released bird means. Readings differ here:**
  - Gill (on v. 7) and Henry: the leper's freedom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-14.html and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_014.cfm
  - Pulpit (on vv. 1–32): either uncleanness carried off as with the scapegoat, or the leper's new freedom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-14.html
  - Coffman reports Meyrick's objection, based on v. 53: the "freedom" reading must be wrong, since a house can't do anything with liberty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/14-53.html
  - Coffman himself takes the slain bird as Christ's death and the freed bird as his resurrection, linked to the two Day of Atonement goats. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-14.html
  - Biblehub's study note reads it as removal of impurity, like the scapegoat (Lev 16:10). https://biblehub.com/study/leviticus/14-53.htm
- **Christ in the rite (common evangelical reading).** Two birds stand for death and new life, substitution, and Christ's blood. Hyssop shows cleansing must be applied personally. Believers are now "God's house" (Heb 3:6). https://biblehub.com/leviticus/14-49.htm
- The study note on v. 53 also presents the priest as foreshadowing Christ the mediator (Heb 9:11–14). https://biblehub.com/study/leviticus/14-53.htm
- **Catholic translation (only an indirect Catholic source found).** The Douay-Rheims renders v. 53 "he shall pray for the house," where other versions say "make atonement." https://biblehub.com/leviticus/14-53.htm
- **Debated popular teaching (Benny Hinn, reported by Everett on the parallel vv. 4–7).** Hinn reads each item as the cross:
  - cedar = the cross; scarlet = Jesus' robe; hyssop = the vinegar sponge
  - water with blood = his pierced side
  - seven sprinklings = seven times Jesus shed blood in his Passion

  Everett reports this without assessing it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/leviticus-14.html
- A sanitary-plus-symbolic reading appears in the Biblical Illustrator sermons on Biblehub. They say house-leprosy was sent "in mercy and not in judgment" to expose hidden unhealthiness, and they call the cleansing rules a thorough sanitary system. https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/14-49.htm

### vv. 54–57 (summary of chs. 13–14)
- Gill: these verses sum up all the laws on the various kinds of leprosy in chs. 13–14. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-14.html
- Constable: the verses close the section and state its purpose. The emphasis is on God providing cleansing so that something corrupt can be set apart for use again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-14.html
- Guzik: these verses sum up the laws of leprosy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-14/

---

**Gaps:**
- **Protestant traditions:** where the pages labeled commentators, the only ones were Gill (Calvinist/Baptist) and Constable (dispensational). The other differences I found are between individual commentators, not documented positions of the Reformed, Baptist, Methodist or Lutheran traditions.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** only Haydock and the Douay wording; nothing Orthodox.
- **Modern scholarship:** limited to the NET notes, plus the Knobel and Lange debates as older commentators report them.

Running more searches later would fill these in, especially the full Enduring Word page for vv. 30–57, Biblehub's per-verse Ellicott and Pulpit pages for vv. 54–57, and the Catholic and Orthodox sites.
